test_cases.question: A 62-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of progressive dysphagia that initially involved solid foods and later progressed to difficulty swallowing liquids. He also reported unintentional weight loss of approximately 8 kg over this period. He denied odynophagia, hematemesis, or prior history of gastroesophageal reflux disease. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed mild normocytic anemia. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated an irregular, circumferential thickening of the mid-esophagus with luminal narrowing. A barium swallow study showed an irregular narrowing with shouldered edges. There was no evidence of distant metastasis on imaging.
test_cases.ground_truth_reasoning:
Progressive dysphagia suggests esophageal malignancy.
Weight loss supports a malignant process.
contexts: Esophageal carcinoma commonly presents with progressive dysphagia that advances from solids to liquids and is frequently associated with weight loss.
Benign strictures are usually related to chronic reflux or caustic injury and are less commonly associated with marked weight loss.
test_cases.answer_reasoning: Significant weight loss further supports a malignant etiology.

test_cases.question: A 30-year-old man presented with several months of pain and a tender, localized swelling on the left side of his hard palate. Panoramic radiography and CT were unremarkable for bony disease. MRI demonstrated a small, well-circumscribed soft-tissue lesion in the palatal mucosa with high T2 signal. Empiric antibiotics produced no improvement; an incisional biopsy revealed numerous disorganized nerve bundles.
test_cases.ground_truth_reasoning:
Lack of response to antibiotics argues against infection.
High T2 signal on MRI suggests a soft-tissue nerve lesion.
Biopsy shows disorganized nerve bundles characteristic of traumatic neuroma.
contexts: Traumatic neuromas arise from nerve injury and histologically show disorganized axonal sprouts and nerve bundle proliferation.
Peripheral nerve tumors often have high T2 signal on MRI while CT and radiographs can be normal if confined to soft tissue.
test_cases.answer_reasoning: MRI high T2 signal and biopsy showing disorganized nerve bundles support a nerve-derived lesion.

test_cases.question: A 23-year-old woman presented with 12 hours of right lower quadrant abdominal pain, anorexia, low-grade fever (38.2°C), and nausea. On exam she has localized tenderness and guarding in the right iliac fossa. Labs show leukocytosis (WBC 14.2 x10^9/L). Right lower quadrant ultrasound demonstrates a non-compressible, blind-ended tubular structure 8 mm in diameter with peri-appendiceal fluid.
test_cases.ground_truth_reasoning:
Focal right lower quadrant pain with guarding is classic for appendicitis.
Leukocytosis and low-grade fever support an inflammatory/infectious process.
Ultrasound shows a non-compressible tubular structure consistent with appendiceal inflammation.
contexts: Acute appendicitis typically presents with periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant, localized tenderness, fever, and leukocytosis.
Ultrasound can demonstrate a non-compressible tubular structure and peri-appendiceal fluid consistent with appendicitis.
test_cases.answer_reasoning: Localizing right lower quadrant pain, fever, and ultrasound findings are consistent with appendicitis.

test_cases.question: A 58-year-old woman developed sudden onset dyspnea and pleuritic right-sided chest pain 6 hours after a transatlantic flight. She is tachycardic and mildly hypoxic on room air. D-dimer is elevated and CT pulmonary angiography shows a segmental filling defect in the right lower-lobe pulmonary artery.
test_cases.ground_truth_reasoning:
Sudden dyspnea with pleuritic chest pain and hypoxia is suggestive of pulmonary embolism.
Recent prolonged immobilization (long-haul flight) is a risk factor for venous thromboembolism.
CT pulmonary angiography demonstrating a filling defect confirms pulmonary embolism.
contexts: Pulmonary embolism commonly presents with acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, and hypoxia.
Long-haul travel and recent prolonged immobilization increase the risk of venous thromboembolism.
test_cases.answer_reasoning: Acute dyspnea after a long flight and clinical hypoxia strongly point to pulmonary embolism.

test_cases.question: A 70-year-old man was found with sudden-onset left-sided weakness and slurred speech starting one hour ago. On arrival he has left facial droop, 0/5 power in his left leg, and expressive aphasia. Non-contrast head CT shows no hemorrhage; diffusion-weighted MRI demonstrates an acute focal diffusion restriction in the right MCA territory.
test_cases.ground_truth_reasoning:
Sudden focal neurological deficits localizing to a vascular territory indicate acute ischemia.
DWI MRI demonstrating restricted diffusion in the right MCA territory confirms an acute ischemic infarct.
contexts: Ischemic stroke presents with sudden focal neurological deficits, often localized to a specific vascular territory.
Diffusion-weighted MRI detects acute ischemic infarction as areas of restricted diffusion.
test_cases.answer_reasoning: Focal sudden-onset neuro deficits are typical of an acute stroke.
